title: Sulayman's du'a
hookLine: inspire me to be grateful, and to do good that pleases You (27:19)

lines: AN ARMY IN THE VALLEY OF THE ANTS.
cards: An army on the march: people, jinn and birds, the Qur'an says, all in their ranks, and at the front a king, Sulayman, the one the Bible calls Solomon. They come to a valley full of ants.
And one ant calls out to the others: get into your homes, or Sulayman and his soldiers will crush you without even noticing. Surah twenty-seven says Sulayman heard her.
He had been taught the speech of birds, and here he understands an ant. The king at the head of that army stops, and smiles.

teach.h: HE SMILED, LAUGHING AT HER WORDS.
teach.b: What he does next is surah twenty-seven, verse nineteen. He smiled, laughing at her words, and prayed.
In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord, arouse me to be thankful for Thy favour wherewith Thou hast favoured me and my parents, and to do good that shall be pleasing unto Thee."
The word Pickthall renders arouse me is awzi'ni.

teach.h: AWZI'NI: KEEP ME AT IT, INSPIRE ME.
teach.b: Translators give it as inspire me, keep me devoted, or urge me on. Either way, Sulayman doesn't trust himself to stay grateful on his own. He asks to be kept at it.
Count what he has: a kingdom, an army, the speech of birds. And the moment that gift shows him a tiny creature worried about her family, his first reaction isn't pride.
It's thanks, and a request for help to keep thanking.
Notice who he includes: me and my parents. The gift that let him hear an ant didn't start with him.
Later in the same surah, when a throne is brought to him in the blink of an eye, he says, in effect, this is from my Lord's bounty, to test me whether I give thanks or turn ungrateful.
So for Sulayman, a skill is also a question.

teach.h: THE SAME WORDS AGAIN, AT FORTY.
teach.b: One more detail: nearly the same words come back in surah forty-six, from an ordinary person who reaches forty years old. The king's prayer turns out to be a prayer for anyone who has been given anything.

how: Some Muslims say the du'a of 27:19, rabbi awzi'ni an ashkura ni'mataka, in moments of success or gratitude; the similar words of 46:15 are also taught as a du'a for parents and children.

o: keep me grateful, for me and my parents
let me understand every creature's speech
make my army strong enough to win

p: warned the others to go home
inspire me, keep me at it

s: when Sulayman heard the ant, his first reaction was to give thanks
he smiled, laughed, and prayed to be kept grateful.
Sulayman's du'a asks only for himself
he gives thanks for favor on him and on his parents.
the same request appears elsewhere in the Qur'an
surah forty-six gives nearly the same words to a person reaching forty.

games.q: you are Sulayman, a king at the head of an army. you've just understood an ant warning her people about you. what do you do?
o: order the army to march on.
smile, and ask to be kept grateful.
boast to your soldiers about your gift.
games.why: he smiled, laughing at her words, and prayed: arouse me to be thankful. a gift became a reason to thank, not to boast.

practice: Pick one thing you can do, cook a dish without a recipe, calm a crying baby, fix a sink, make a stranger laugh, and trace it back to who taught you or gave you the time to learn it.
If you pray, thank Allah for the skill and the people behind it, in your own words or with Sulayman's; if you don't, simply hold the skill and the people with it, gratefully.

wordCard.voice: Sulayman's du'a. A king who heard an ant, smiled, and asked to be kept grateful, for himself and for his parents, and to do good that pleases Allah. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: inspire me, keep me at it (27:19). Pickthall: arouse me.

carryVoice: Your line: inspire me to be grateful. A gift is also a question. That's day six hundred ninety-four.

sources.q: My Lord, arouse me to be thankful for Thy favour wherewith Thou hast favoured me and my parents, and to do good that shall be pleasing unto Thee
